settings.content: The cross-section decides whether a ring is worn or taken off

settings.heading: The Profile Is the Cross-Section
settings.body:
The profile is the cross-section of the band: the shape you would see if the ring were sliced cleanly in half. It determines how the ring feels, how it catches light and how it sits beside an engagement ring.

It is also the single most under-considered decision in buying a wedding ring. A ring with the wrong profile is often quietly taken off and left in a drawer. The right one becomes almost invisible in daily wear, which is exactly what you want from something worn for fifty years.

settings.cells: Traditional court | Domed outside and domed inside; soft and classic | Most hands, daily comfort, traditional bands
Slight court | A lower, gentler dome with a refined silhouette | Delicate engagement rings; softness without height
Engagement match | A court-related profile shaped to pair cleanly | Straight bands beside solitaires and low settings
D-shape | Domed outside and flat inside; traditional and substantial | Classic British bands and heavier plain rings
Flat | Flat outside and flat inside; clean and architectural | Modern wider bands and design-led wearers
Flat court | Flat outside with a curved comfort interior | A modern look with easier daily wear
Edged flat court | Flat court with bevelled edges that catch light | Crisp contemporary bands and mixed finishes
Edged court | Court band with defined bevelled edges | Refined classic bands with subtle detail
Concave | Outer face curves inward for a distinctive look | Minimalist and contemporary designs

settings.intro: Width is measured across the top of the band, the part you see looking down at the hand.
settings.heading: How Wide, and What It Does
A Note on 1.5mm Bands
settings.body:
A 1.5mm band is delicate and minimal, and that is precisely its appeal. But bands at or below 1.5mm carry a higher risk of bending or distorting under heavy impact, depending on alloy purity and lifestyle.

For active daily wear, a minimum of 2.0 to 2.5mm offers significantly greater structural strength. If you love the look of the finest band, we would rather tell you this now than reshape it for you in two years.

settings.heading: Depth is the other half
settings.body: Depth is the thickness from the inside of the finger to the outer surface, typically around 1.5 to 2mm. Deeper bands feel more substantial and wear longer before losing definition, but sit higher off the finger.

settings.heading: Shallower sits closer
settings.body: A shallower band sits nearer the hand and pairs more easily with an engagement ring, but it should never feel flimsy. On a stone-set band, depth also determines whether the stones can be held securely.

settings.heading: Proportion is personal
settings.body: The same width looks different on different hands. A narrow band lengthens the finger; a wider band balances long fingers and makes a stronger statement.

settings.heading: Balance against the engagement ring
settings.body: A slim solitaire can be overwhelmed by a heavy band, while a larger or architectural engagement ring may need more width to look balanced beside it.

settings.heading: When to Consider a Domed Interior
settings.body:
A comfort-fit band has a gently domed inner surface, so it slides over the knuckle more easily and contacts the finger along a slightly narrower area. It is especially useful for wider bands, prominent knuckles, and wearers whose fingers change size during the day.

For bands above around 4mm, comfort fit is usually worth considering. Note that a comfort-fit ring often fits a half size differently from a flat-interior one, which is why we size against the actual profile rather than a generic gauge.

settings.heading: Get the Size Right for the Profile
settings.body: Profile changes fit. A comfort-fit 6mm band and a flat-interior 2mm band in the same nominal size feel quite different on the same finger. We size against the profile you have actually chosen, not a generic gauge.

settings.q: What is the most comfortable wedding ring profile?
settings.a: Traditional court for most people. It is domed inside and out, so there are no edges against the finger and nothing to catch on the adjacent one. Flat court is the modern alternative: a flat outer face with the same curved interior.

settings.q: What width wedding ring should a man wear?
settings.a: There is no rule, but 4 to 6mm covers most preferences. Larger hands generally carry more width comfortably. The stronger determinant is what they are used to: someone who has never worn a ring will notice 6mm considerably more than someone who has.

settings.q: Should the wedding band match the engagement ring's width?
settings.a: Same or very close usually looks most intentional beside a solitaire. If you want contrast, make it obvious. The one thing to avoid is the almost-match, where a band is only slightly different and reads as accidental.

settings.q: Can I try profiles before ordering?
settings.a: Yes, and we would encourage it above 4mm or for anyone who has not worn a ring before. We keep a full range of sample rings which we can show you in person or send to your home.

settings.q: Is a thicker ring more durable?
settings.a: Generally yes. Depth does more for durability than width. A narrow but deep band will hold its shape better than a wide but shallow one, which is why we would rather add depth than width on a fine ring.
